The count is read directly from the selection set in Rust, so it is cheaper than `len(get_selected_node_ids())` when you only need the size. It is a quick way to check what a selection rule matched before acting on it -- for example, to make sure a selection is not empty (or not the whole graph) before calling `delete_nodes_ws()`, or to report how many nodes passed a filter. The selection itself is not changed. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of selected nodes; `0` if nothing is selected. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a complete graph of 10 nodes, every node has degree `9`, so all of them meet a `min_degree=5` threshold: ::: {#deeea37e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_full_graph(10) .select_nodes_by_degree(min_degree=5) ) graph.count_selected_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10 ``` ::: ::: Because the count reflects the selection at the moment it is called, it can track a selection as it changes. In a 6-node path, the one-hop neighborhood of the first node has 2 nodes, and inverting it leaves the other 4: ::: {#bbaf688b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(6) first = graph.get_node_creation_order()[0] graph.select_nodes_in_neighborhood(first, k=1) before = graph.count_selected_nodes() graph.invert_node_selection() after = graph.count_selected_nodes() (before, after) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (2, 4) ``` ::: :::
